question: Which enzyme allows HIV to copy its RNA into DNA inside a host cell?
explanation: Reverse transcriptase is the specific retroviral enzyme that converts viral RNA into DNA. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h1)

question: What is the main job of the gp120 protein on the HIV surface?

options.A: It prevents the host immune system from producing antibodies
options.B: It digests the host cell nuclear membrane to release viral genes
options.C: It binds specifically to receptors on the surface of target immune cells
options.D: It forms the inner capsid core that protects the viral RNA strands

explanation: Glycoprotein 120 acts like a key that attaches to CD4 receptors on target cells so the virus can enter. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h1)

question: Which main receptor on immune cells does the HIV gp120 protein attach to?
explanation: The CD4 molecule serves as the primary binding site for the viral gp120 protein. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h2)

question: What is the role of coreceptors like CCR5 during HIV entry into a cell?

options.A: They neutralize antibodies produced by nearby B-lymphocytes
options.B: They transport the integrated provirus out of the host cell nucleus
options.C: They trigger the shape change needed for the virus and cell membranes to fuse
options.D: They destroy the viral capsid before reverse transcription starts

explanation: Coreceptor engagement is a necessary step that exposes gp41 to help the viral and host membranes merge. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h2)

question: What does the viral integrase enzyme do during HIV replication?

options.A: It cuts long viral protein chains into functional pieces
options.B: It transcribes viral RNA back into cellular cytoplasm
options.C: It copies host DNA to create viral envelope proteins
options.D: It inserts viral DNA into the host cell genome

explanation: Integrase permanently places the copied viral DNA into the host's own chromosomes as a provirus. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h3)

question: Why does ongoing HIV replication cause CD4+ cell counts to steadily drop?

options.A: Infected cells are directly destroyed by lysis, cell suicide, and killer T-cells
options.B: Circulating antibodies neutralize and trap all available lymphocytes in lymph nodes
options.C: The bone marrow completely stops producing any white blood cells
options.D: Mature T-cells transform into malignant cancer cells due to genetic damage

explanation: Multiple destruction processes combine to deplete CD4+ T-cells faster than the body can make new ones. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h3)

question: What is the term for the flu-like illness that happens a few weeks after catching HIV?
explanation: Acute retroviral syndrome is the body's reaction to high amounts of the virus circulating early in the infection. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h4)

question: What clinical finding marks the shift from chronic HIV infection to full-blown AIDS?

options.A: Permanent stabilization of the patient's immune system
options.B: CD4+ T-cell count dropping below 200 cells/mm³
options.C: Complete disappearance of viral RNA from peripheral blood
options.D: Development of resistance to all available drug classes

explanation: A CD4 count falling below 200 cells/mm³ marks the official clinical threshold for an AIDS diagnosis. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h4)

question: Which WHO clinical stage of HIV features no symptoms or just swollen lymph nodes?
explanation: Stage 1 is the earliest phase where patients generally feel well, other than having persistent swollen lymph glands. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h5)

question: Why does the WHO often use clinical symptoms to stage HIV instead of lab tests in some areas?

options.A: Patients refuse blood draws during routine outpatient clinic visits
options.B: Clinical staging is scientifically more accurate than laboratory testing
options.C: Laboratory tests cannot detect HIV antibodies in tropical environments
options.D: CD4 cell counts and viral load tests may not be immediately available everywhere

explanation: Clinical staging offers a practical guide to start treatment when advanced lab equipment is missing. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h5)

question: How does advanced HIV infection affect B-lymphocyte function?

options.A: They clear the viral reservoir from lymph node tissue completely
options.B: They stop producing any immunoglobulins entirely
options.C: They show high antibody levels but fail to mount new effective responses
options.D: They transform into functional CD4+ T-cells to replace lost cells

explanation: Advanced HIV causes general B-cell confusion, leading to high background antibodies but poor defense against new threats. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h6)

question: What is the main danger when the immune system collapses in late-stage HIV?

options.A: Spontaneous clearance of the viral genome from host chromosomes
options.B: Immediate regeneration of damaged thymic tissue and lymph nodes
options.C: Loss of control over common germs and hidden infections
options.D: Activation of hyper-functional cytotoxic cells that attack healthy organs

explanation: Without immune surveillance, opportunistic germs easily take over because the body's defenses are down. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h6)

question: Which fungus commonly causes meningitis in patients with advanced AIDS?
explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast that frequently causes serious brain and spinal cord infections in people with weak immunity. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h7)

question: Why are AIDS patients more likely to develop cancers like Kaposi's sarcoma?

options.A: Circulating HIV virions integrate into epithelial cells and cause cancer
options.B: The immune system can no longer control cancer-causing viruses and abnormal cells
options.C: Antiretroviral drugs directly mutate healthy tissue into aggressive tumors
options.D: Nutritional deficiencies completely shut down normal cellular DNA repair

explanation: A weak immune system can no longer suppress abnormal cell growth or viruses that trigger tumors. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h7)
